stem.text: The function \( f \) is differentiable on the closed interval \( [0, 6] \). The table gives selected values of \( f \). \[ \begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 2 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline f(x) & 2 & -3 & 4 & 1 \end{array} \]

parts.prompt: Must there be a value \( c \), with \( 0 < c < 2 \), for which \( f(c) = 0 \)? Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: f is differentiable on [0, 6], so it is continuous on [0, 2].
By the Intermediate Value Theorem such a c exists.

points.criterion: States that f is continuous on [0, 2] because f is differentiable there.
Shows that 0 is strictly between f(2) = -3 and f(0) = 2 and answers yes, with continuity cited.

parts.prompt: Explain why the equation \( f(x) = -1 \) must have at least two solutions in the open interval \( (0, 6) \).
parts.answer_latex: \text{at least one solution in } (0,2) \text{ and one in } (2,5)

worked_solution.text: f is continuous on [0, 6] because it is differentiable there.
-1 also lies between f(2) and f(5).
The Intermediate Value Theorem gives a solution in each of the two disjoint intervals.

points.criterion: States that f is continuous on the intervals used because f is differentiable on [0, 6].
Places -1 strictly between f(0) and f(2) and strictly between f(2) and f(5), concluding there is a solution in each of the two separate intervals.

parts.prompt: Let \( g(x) = f(x) + x \). Must there be a value \( c \), with \( 2 < c < 5 \), for which \( g(c) = 5 \)? Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: g is a sum of two functions continuous on [2, 5], since f is differentiable.
5 lies between the endpoint values, so such a c exists.

points.criterion: States that g is continuous on [2, 5] because f is differentiable (hence continuous) and x is continuous.
Computes g(2) = -1 and g(5) = 9, shows 5 is strictly between them and answers yes.
